text: You've built a multi-year roadmap, a way to prioritize when resources are limited, and a business case that got it funded. This last lesson in the chapter is the guardrail against the failure that can undo all three: shipping something that checks a compliance box and gets labeled zero trust, without actually reducing the implicit trust or the risk the whole roadmap was built to reduce.

Four patterns show up repeatedly. A product gets bought and licensed, but every existing access path is allow-listed to avoid breaking anything, so real access barely changes. A policy gets written but deployed in report-only mode and never flipped to actually block anything, often indefinitely. A roadmap item closes because the project plan says it's done, not because anyone checked whether the thing it was supposed to fix is fixed. And a project's scope quietly narrows to whatever was easy, then gets reported without that qualification.

Here's the difference in practice. The theater version of a status update says 'we deployed micro-segmentation' — shipped, done, box checked. The real version says a specific compromised account reached forty systems in January and reaches three systems in June, same account, same privileges, measured after rollout. Only the second one is proof the control did anything.

The fix for every one of those four patterns is the same question, asked at the end of the initiative, not just the start: is there measurably less implicit trust, and is the blast radius of a plausible incident actually smaller — not 'this tool could do that in theory,' but a real access path that existed before and doesn't exist now. If an initiative can't produce that comparison, it isn't done yet, whatever the project plan says.

That closes this chapter. You now have a sequenced roadmap, a way to prioritize it under real constraints, a funded business case, and the test that keeps every one of those honest. The next chapter is the capstone: designing and defending a full zero trust architecture for a hybrid enterprise, under exactly this kind of scrutiny.
